items.title: An AI legal team for software companies
items.pitch: Terms, privacy policies, data processing agreements and the record of every vendor that touches customer data, drafted, kept current and reviewed by a lawyer.
capabilities: Drafts and updates terms, privacy policies and data processing agreements as the product changes
Reviews vendor and customer contracts and flags what needs a lawyer
Tracks new rules, like the EU AI Act, and says what each one changes for you
items.whyMotir: Every model provider Motir adds needs a data processing agreement and a recorded legal basis for sending customer data to it. Today that is slow, manual work.
items.whoElse: Every software company that handles customer data, which is all of them.

items.title: An AI finance team for startups
items.pitch: Price the plans, bill for usage, file the taxes and pay the vendors, from one place that understands what each customer actually costs.
capabilities: Sets plan prices from real costs: model calls, machine time, storage
Reconciles usage billing and files sales tax and VAT in every country you sell to
Pays vendors, tracks runway and closes the books each month
items.whyMotir: Motir resells model calls and machine minutes at a margin. Pricing a plan means knowing the cost of every credit, in every currency, after tax.
items.whoElse: Every usage-priced software startup, from its first invoice to its first audit.

items.title: AI security and compliance, from the evidence
items.pitch: SOC 2 and ISO 27001 evidence collected from the code, the cloud and the project itself, and security questionnaires answered from it.
capabilities: Collects evidence from repositories, cloud accounts and the project's history
Answers customer security questionnaires from that evidence, with sources
Watches for drift and opens a work item when a control slips
items.whyMotir: A business customer asks for a security review before it signs. Every answer is somewhere in Motir's code and records, and finding it takes days we would rather spend building.
items.whoElse: Every software company selling to a business big enough to ask.

items.title: AI support that knows the product
items.pitch: Answers customers from the docs, the code and the live state of the product, and turns a real bug into a planned work item instead of a reply.
capabilities: Answers from documentation, code and the customer's own account
Hands a real defect to the engineering team as a planned work item, with the evidence
Learns from every answer a person corrects
items.whyMotir: Motir's users ask about agents, models, credits and repositories. A good answer needs the code and the account, not a help-center search.
items.whoElse: Every developer-tool and B2B software company with more customers than support staff.

items.title: AI localization that keeps up with the product
items.pitch: Translates the interface, the docs and the emails as they change, keeps every term consistent, and has a native speaker review what matters.
capabilities: Translates each change as it lands, not in a yearly project
Keeps a glossary so a term means one thing everywhere
Sends the risky strings, legal text and pricing to a native reviewer
items.whyMotir: Motir ships in English and Chinese, and every release changes hundreds of strings. Keeping both right by hand does not scale to a third language.
items.whoElse: Every software company that wants customers outside its home country.

items.title: AI growth for B2B software
items.pitch: Turns what a team ships into launch posts, changelog announcements, comparison pages and search-ready docs, and measures what brings customers.
capabilities: Writes the announcement for each release from the work that shipped
Builds and refreshes the pages people search for before they buy
Shows which pages and posts bring customers, not just visitors
items.whyMotir: Motir ships every day, in public. Turning that into posts and pages people find takes a marketing team we do not have.
items.whoElse: Every B2B software company that ships faster than it can tell anyone.

items.title: Make a store visible to AI shoppers
items.pitch: Gets a small store's products found and recommended by the AI assistants people now shop through, and shows how often each product is picked.

evidence.claim: Traffic from AI assistants to US retail sites rose 693% in the 2025 holiday season and converted 31% better than other traffic.
evidence.sourceName: Adobe Analytics, via Digital Commerce 360, January 2026

items.gap: The funded players sell to large brands and big catalogs. Millions of small stores have nothing yet, and the window is short.

items.title: Stop returns before they happen
items.pitch: Spots the order bought in three sizes to send two back, answers the fit question before checkout, and scores each return for fraud.

evidence.claim: Shoppers were expected to return $849.9 billion of goods in 2025, 19.3% of online sales, and 9% of returns are fraudulent.
evidence.sourceName: National Retail Federation and Happy Returns, October 2025

items.gap: Return platforms handle the return once it starts. Preventing it, for stores below enterprise size, is barely served.

items.title: APIs that update their customers' code
items.pitch: When an API makes a breaking change, the provider opens the pull request that migrates each customer's code, instead of sending an email.

evidence.claim: On Y Combinator's Fall 2026 Requests for Startups: API providers shouldn't just announce changes; they should apply them.
evidence.sourceName: Y Combinator, Requests for Startups, Fall 2026

items.gap: Dependency bots only bump version numbers, and SDK generators don't touch customer code. Agents can now edit unfamiliar code well enough to open the pull request.

items.title: AI cost by feature and by customer
items.pitch: Splits the AI bill by feature and by customer, sets budgets, and shows finance and engineering the margin of every plan in one view.

evidence.claim: 79% of finance leaders report AI cost overruns, and only 15% can calculate the return on AI spend without significant bottlenecks.
evidence.sourceName: DoiT and Sapio Research, survey of 500 finance leaders, February 2026

items.gap: Cloud cost tools are built around the cloud bill, and AI observability tools are built for developers. Neither gives finance a margin per feature.

items.title: The AI transparency kit
items.pitch: A drop-in kit that tells users they're talking to an AI, marks generated content in a machine-readable way and labels deepfakes, as the EU now requires.

evidence.claim: The EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026, with systems already on the market given until 2 December 2026, and fines of up to €15 million or 3% of worldwide turnover.
evidence.sourceName: Jones Walker, AI Law Blog, July 2026

items.gap: Content-marking vendors serve enterprises or one platform. A small app maker has no simple way to comply before the deadline.

items.title: A first tutor for young children
items.pitch: A voice tutor at home that teaches four-to-eight-year-olds to read, write and count, one child at a time, at the child's own pace.

evidence.claim: On Y Combinator's Fall 2026 Requests for Startups as "The Primer", noting the cost of the AI per child is falling about ten times a year.
evidence.sourceName: Y Combinator, Requests for Startups, Fall 2026

items.gap: Ello, the funded AI tutor for this age, teaches reading only, and the best-known AI tutors are built for schools, not homes.

items.title: A career coach for people who pay for themselves
items.pitch: Coaching and practice conversations for the job you want next, for the many workers whose employer won't pay for training.

evidence.claim: Valence raised a $50 million Series B for AI coaching, after more than a million coaching conversations, showing AI coaching works when employers buy it.

items.gap: AI coaching is sold only to employers, and learning platforms sell courses, not coaching. Nobody serves the person who pays for themselves.

items.title: Treatment options for vet clinics
items.pitch: During the exam, turns one diagnosis into two or three priced treatment plans with a payment plan attached, so the pet gets care the owner can afford.

evidence.claim: 94% of vets say cost stops recommended care, and 81% say they offer alternatives, yet 73% of pet owners say they were never offered a cheaper plan.
evidence.sourceName: Gallup and PetSmart Charities, survey of 933 vets, 2025

items.gap: Vet AI tools write the visit notes and practice software books the visits. None turns a case into priced options.

items.title: A care team app for families
items.pitch: Shares medicines, tasks and appointments across the family looking after a parent, and explains each care task in plain words.

evidence.claim: 63 million Americans are family caregivers, about 45% more than in 2015. More than half do medical or nursing tasks, and only 20% have been trained.
evidence.sourceName: AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, July 2025

items.gap: Care coordination is sold to employers as a benefit, or comes with paid carers. The free apps families use are basic.
